content.text: An average response time describes almost no real request. Latency is skewed: most requests are fast and a few are very slow, so the mean lands somewhere between them and hides the slow ones. Use the median for the typical request and p95 or p99 for the slow ones, record latency as a histogram so you can compute percentiles across servers, and never average percentiles.

The API dashboard has one latency line, the average, and it has been flat and green all month. Support sees a different picture: some customers say the order page hangs for a few seconds, then loads as if nothing happened. The team opens the dashboard while one of those complaints is coming in. The average hasn't moved.
The common misconception
The belief: average response time is a good measure of how fast a service feels. If the average is low, users are waiting a short time.

It's an easy number to trust. It's one value, it's cheap, and every metrics system can produce it: the Prometheus docs note that histograms and summaries track a count and a sum of observations, "allowing you to calculate the average of the observed values." Google's SRE book itself uses an example target where "our average search request latency should be less than 100 milliseconds," before explaining why it prefers percentiles. And for data shaped like a bell curve, the mean really is the typical value.
The half-truth: the mean is accurate about the total time spent. It just doesn't describe any one user's wait, because latency isn't shaped like a bell curve.
What actually happens
Latency is skewed

The article on logs, metrics and traces put latency first among the four golden signals; the question here is how to read it. Most requests take the fast path, and a few hit a cache miss, a lock or a retry. The SRE book explains why the shape is lopsided: "no request can have a response in less than 0 ms", while a slow request can take many times longer than a typical one. So "we cannot assume that the mean and the median are the same—or even close to each other!" A handful of very slow requests drags the mean up, away from where most requests are.
Percentiles describe the shape
A
percentile

answers a direct question: what latency are p% of requests at or under? The SRE book recommends thinking of metrics "as distributions rather than averages", and explains what each end tells you: "a high-order percentile, such as the 99th or 99.9th, shows you a plausible worst-case value, while using the 50th percentile (also known as the median) emphasizes the typical case."
The tail reaches more users than its share

One slow request in a hundred sounds rare. But a page often waits for several backend calls, and the slowest one sets the pace. The SRE book's warning: "If your users depend on several such web services to render their page, the 99th percentile of one backend can easily become the median response of your frontend." That's why
tail latency
deserves its own line on the dashboard.
The average hides changes in the tail

The SRE book shows a system whose tail latency changed a lot during one day, while "monitoring and alerting based only on the average latency would show no change in behavior." In its footnote, the conclusion is blunt: if you're not measuring the distribution, "the idea that most of your requests are near the mean is just hopeful thinking."
The fix: report percentiles, not the mean
Here are two simulated days of 10,000 requests each, generated with a fixed seed and run with
dotnet run latency.cs
on .NET 10. On day A every request takes 20 to 200 ms. On day B, 95% of requests hit a cache and the rest miss:

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
✅ Right

content.text: By the mean, the two days are the same. By the percentiles, they're two different services. On day A, the typical request takes 110 ms and even the slowest 1% stay under 200 ms. On day B, the typical request is twice as fast, but 1 in 100 requests waits more than 1.7 seconds. Notice that p95 missed it too: with about 5% slow requests, the 95th percentile still lands on a fast one. Track p99 next to p95.
Counting the same requests into buckets about 3 times apart, as the SRE book suggests, shows why:

Day B's mean of 109 ms falls in a bucket with no requests at all. In the same run, not one of its requests was within 10% of the mean, while 470 took longer than 500 ms. That's the customer who complained, and the average can't show them.

blocks.title: Record a histogram, compute percentiles when you query

content.text: A
histogram

counts requests per latency bucket, and the SRE book recommends exactly that: "collect request counts bucketed by latencies (suitable for rendering a histogram), rather than actual latencies." Prometheus histograms keep the distribution so you can "calculate arbitrary quantiles over arbitrary time windows" later, and its docs show putting bucket boundaries around a target such as serving 95% of requests within 300 ms.
A summary computes percentiles inside each instance, and Prometheus warns that "you cannot aggregate quantiles". Its docs mark
avg(http_request_duration_seconds{quantile="0.95"})
as BAD: "averaging the quantiles yields statistically nonsensical values." Sum the histogram buckets of all instances first, then compute the percentile from the total with
histogram_quantile
How to apply it in your project
Search your dashboards and alerts for average or mean latency. Replace each one with p50, p95 and p99 on the same graph, so the typical case and the tail are side by side.
Use your metrics library's histogram type for request durations, with bucket boundaries around the latencies that matter to you. The SRE book suggests spacing them "approximately exponentially".
To get the p99 of a service with many instances, add up their bucket counts and compute the percentile from the sum. Never average the per-instance p99.
Alert on p99 for user-facing endpoints, not on the mean. The SRE book adds that measuring p99 over a short window "can give a very early signal of saturation."
Key takeaways

items.text: The mean of latencies describes almost no request; on our day B, none was within 10% of it.
Latency is skewed, so use p50 for the typical request and p95 and p99 for the slow ones.
Two very different days can have the same mean; percentiles tell them apart.
Record latency as a histogram, add up buckets across servers, and never average percentiles.
The tail reaches more users than its share, so alert on p99, not on the average.
